children: , the integrated-energy company and major LNG trader, warned that the global energy market is running through its remaining cushions after losing roughly 36 million metric tons of LNG and 1.6 billion barrels of crude oil and condensates since the Middle East conflict began. The U.S. shares were nearly flat at $95.51.

Shell's chief economist said weaker Chinese demand, inventory drawdowns, flexible shipping, spare pipeline capacity and rising production from the Americas helped soften the first wave of disruption. That protection is thinning. Even if key energy routes reopen, damaged infrastructure and supply-chain bottlenecks could keep the market tight well into 2027, while Europe heads toward winter with unusually low gas inventories.

That environment can increase the strategic value of Shell's LNG portfolio, shipping reach and global trading network, but high prices cut both ways. Asian buyers have already shifted toward coal, nuclear power and domestic gas as LNG became less affordable, showing how quickly demand can retreat when energy costs surge. The valuation picture adds another caution flag: the chart shows Shell at $95.51 versus a GF Value estimate of $82.90, leaving the shares 15.21% above that benchmark. Volatility may create more trading opportunities for Shell, but the stock price already reflects a meaningful premium while affordability remains a hard ceiling on demand.

title: Shell Warns 36 Million Lost LNG Tons Are Exhausting Market Buffers
